title: Tristan und Isolde: Prelude and Liebestod
hook: A chord that longs to resolve, and waits almost twenty minutes to do it.

painting.title: Tristan and Isolde (Death)
painting.collection: Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao
painting.pairingNote: Painted by a Spanish friend of Wagner who devoted his later career to Wagner’s characters, it shows the lovers united in death, the moment of the Liebestod.

facts: *Tristan und Isolde* is an opera in three acts, composed between 1857 and 1859 in Zurich, Venice and Lucerne. Two lovers, bound by a love potion and by a love they cannot live out, find union only in death. It was first staged in Munich on 10 June 1865.
Wagner was reading the philosopher Schopenhauer, for whom desire is endless and never satisfied. He was also in love with Mathilde Wesendonck, the wife of his patron.

The opera’s first chord, the [[tristan-chord|Tristan chord]], does not resolve the way the ear expects. The Prelude keeps reaching for a resolution and never gets it. It comes only at the very end of the opera, in Isolde’s last song.

Wagner himself paired the Prelude with that final scene for concerts. Confusingly, he called the Prelude the “Liebestod” (love-death) and the ending “Transfiguration”. The name Liebestod stuck to the ending after Liszt used it for his piano version in 1867.
This recording is live, from Salzburg in 1987, with the soprano Jessye Norman singing Isolde’s words. The Liebestod is often played without the voice, the soprano’s line given to the orchestra.
bigPicture.inOneLine: longing that never arrives (I), arrival in death (II).

movements.heading: Prelude
movements.title: Prelude (Act I)
movements.summary: Slow waves of longing. A short rising phrase and an unresolved chord are repeated, each time a little higher, then grow into long surges that build to one enormous climax and fall back without ever arriving. Wagner marked it “slow and languishing”.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: the cellos rise by a few notes; woodwinds answer with a strange, unresolved chord, the Tristan chord, and an oboe line that climbs and stops.

mainIdeas.name: The glance
mainIdeas.description: a long, warm melody for the cellos, a little later.

stops.hear: The cellos alone, a short rising phrase; then woodwinds hold a sour, hanging chord; the oboe climbs; silence
stops.happening: The [[tristan-chord|Tristan chord]]. The question the whole opera asks

stops.hear: The same phrase and chord again, a step higher; silence
A third time, higher still; now the music begins to flow
stops.happening: Longing sets the music in motion

stops.hear: The cellos sing a long, warm melody
stops.happening: A new theme, often called “the glance”: the moment the lovers first looked at each other

stops.hear: Wave after wave: the strings swell, the music seems about to arrive, then slips away
stops.happening: Each [[crescendo|crescendo]] falls back before it lands

stops.hear: The full orchestra at its loudest; the brass blaze out the opening chord
The music collapses; the opening phrase returns, broken up in the woodwinds

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Low, quiet strings sink into darkness
stops.happening: In the opera, the curtain would rise here

notice: Sing the cellos’ first three notes back to yourself, then listen for them throughout the Prelude. They are everywhere.

movements.heading: Liebestod
movements.title: Liebestod: "Mild und leise" (Act III)
movements.summary: Tristan has died in Isolde’s arms. She sings over his body, sees him smiling and alive, and is carried away on waves of music until she sinks, as the opera’s last words have it, “unconscious – highest bliss”. The resolution denied in the Prelude finally arrives.

stops.hear: The soprano begins softly, over hushed strings: “Mild und leise wie er lächelt” (“How softly and gently he smiles”)
stops.happening: Isolde’s vision. The melody comes from the lovers’ duet in Act II

stops.hear: The strings begin to rise in waves under the voice
Larger waves; the voice soars above the full orchestra
The climax: the whole orchestra at full power, the voice riding on top; then the music opens out into a radiant major chord
The voice sinks on its last words

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The orchestra alone; an oboe recalls the Tristan chord one last time, and it melts into a calm B major chord

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: It was recorded at a concert in Salzburg in August 1987, while a film about Karajan was being made; he was 79. Jessye Norman sings Isolde.

threads.title: Longing and release
threads.body: The Prelude refuses to resolve; the Liebestod does. Together they make one arc of almost twenty minutes.

threads.title: One chord
threads.body: The Tristan chord opens the Prelude and returns, finally resolved, in the last bars.

threads.title: Waves
threads.body: Both pieces move in surges that build and fall back. Listen to the shape, more than to the tunes.
